#### 🟠 Issue 2: Temporal modeling is semantically incorrect

The Temporal detection creates `CodeElement` nodes whose `name`/`queueName` is the **activity method name** (e.g., `validateOrder`, `chargePayment`), not the **Temporal task queue name** (e.g., `'orders'`). This produces a fundamentally misleading graph.

**What the code does** — for `workflow.ts`:
```typescript
const activities = proxyActivities({ startToCloseTimeout: '30s' });
await activities.validateOrder(orderId);   // → CodeElement node named "validateOrder"
await activities.chargePayment(amount);    // → CodeElement node named "chargePayment"
```
Result: `workflow.ts` gets `PROCESSES` edges to nodes named `validateOrder`, `chargePayment`, `sendConfirmation` — three separate "queue" nodes that don't correspond to any real queue.

**What it should be** — The actual task queue is `'orders'`, defined in `starter.ts`:
```typescript
client.workflow.start(processOrderWorkflow, { taskQueue: 'orders', ... });
```
The `workflow.ts` file **calls** activities (producer role), while workers registered on the `'orders'` task queue are the **consumers**. The current model:
1. Assigns `PROCESSES` edges to the workflow file (it's actually more of a producer/orchestrator)
2. Creates nodes named after function calls, not queues
3. Conflates activity method names with queue names

Additionally, `TEMPORAL_ACTIVITY_RE = /activities\.(\w+)\s*\(/g` will match **any** object named `activities` in any codebase — a common variable name — producing false positives in non-Temporal projects.

[Fix this →](https://claude.ai/code?q=Fix%20Temporal%20queue%20detection%20in%20gitnexus%2Fsrc%2Fcore%2Fingestion%2Fworkers%2Fparse-worker.ts%20on%20branch%20feat%2Fasync-queue-detection.%20Current%20issues%3A%20(1)%20TEMPORAL_ACTIVITY_RE%20matches%20any%20object%20named%20%22activities%22%2C%20not%20just%20Temporal%20proxyActivities.%20Fix%3A%20only%20trigger%20if%20file%20contains%20%22proxyActivities%22%20or%20imports%20from%20%40temporalio.%20(2)%20Activity%20method%20names%20are%20used%20as%20queueName%20but%20they%27re%20function%20names%2C%20not%20queue%20names.%20The%20real%20task%20queue%20name%20is%20in%20taskQueue%20option%20of%20client.workflow.start().%20Consider%20extracting%20that%20instead.%20(3)%20Workflow%20files%20get%20PROCESSES%20edges%20but%20they%20should%20get%20ENQUEUES%20edges%20since%20they%20start%20workflows%20on%20task%20queues.&repo=abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus)

This PR adds regex-based SwiftUI navigation detection and is **functionally correct** — CI is green, all 4197 tests pass. ### Issues Found

#### 🔴 Bug: Worker-path navigations never merged — `parsing-processor.ts`

In `processParsingWithWorkers`, the worker result merge loop pushes all other arrays (`allCalls`, `allRoutes`, `allToolDefs`, etc.) but **never pushes `result.navigations`** into `allNavigations`:

```typescript
// parsing-processor.ts lines 101–110 — navigations is missing!
allImports.push(...result.imports);
allCalls.push(...result.calls);
// ... all other arrays ...
allConstructorBindings.push(...result.constructorBindings);
allTypeEnvBindings.push(...result.typeEnvBindings);
// ← allNavigations.push(...result.navigations) is ABSENT
```

The returned `WorkerExtractedData` at line 129 includes `navigations: allNavigations`, but it will always be an empty array when using workers. This makes the worker extraction in `parse-worker.ts` dead code.

**Why tests still pass:** `pipeline.ts` lines 800–803 run `extractSwiftUINavigations` sequentially for every file regardless of whether workers ran — this masks the bug completely.

[Fix this →](https://claude.ai/code?q=In%20gitnexus%2Fsrc%2Fcore%2Fingestion%2Fparsing-processor.ts%2C%20in%20the%20%60processParsingWithWorkers%60%20function%2C%20the%20worker%20result%20merge%20loop%20(around%20lines%20101-110)%20is%20missing%20%60allNavigations.push(...result.navigations)%60.%20Add%20it%20after%20allToolDefs%20push%20so%20worker-extracted%20navigations%20are%20properly%20accumulated.%20Branch%3A%20feat%2Fswiftui-navigation-graph&repo=abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus)

#### 🔴 Design: Double extraction — `pipeline.ts` + `parse-worker.ts`

`extractSwiftUINavigations` is called in **two places**:

1. Inside `parse-worker.ts` — runs per file in each worker thread
2. Inside `pipeline.ts` lines 800–803 — runs sequentially for **every** file, always, even when workers ran

```typescript
// pipeline.ts — this runs unconditionally, even after worker extraction
for (const file of chunkFiles) {
  extractSwiftUINavigations(file.path, file.content, allNavigations);
}
```

This means if the merge bug above is fixed, every navigation will be extracted twice, doubling the `allNavigations` array. The `seenEdges` dedup in `processSwiftUINavigation` prevents duplicate graph edges, but the raw array would be bloated, and the behavior would be surprising.

**The intent is ambiguous** — the comment says "sequential path" but the code runs regardless of path. The design should pick one place: either extract in workers and propagate (removing the sequential loop), or extract only in the sequential loop (removing it from parse-worker.ts).

[Fix this →](https://claude.ai/code?q=In%20gitnexus%2Fsrc%2Fcore%2Fingestion%2Fpipeline.ts%2C%20the%20SwiftUI%20navigation%20extraction%20loop%20at%20lines%20800-803%20runs%20unconditionally%20even%20when%20workers%20extracted%20navigations.%20Wrap%20it%20in%20%60if%20(!chunkWorkerData)%60%20so%20it%20only%20runs%20on%20the%20sequential%20path%2C%20or%20remove%20the%20worker-path%20extraction%20from%20parse-worker.ts%20entirely.%20Branch%3A%20feat%2Fswiftui-navigation-graph&repo=abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus)

#### 🟡 Limitation: Only "View"-suffixed types detected

All regex patterns match `[A-Z]\w*View\w*` — types must contain "View" in their name:

```typescript
// swiftui-navigation.ts line 18
const NAVIGATION_LINK_RE = /NavigationLink\s*\(\s*(?:destination\s*:\s*)?([A-Z]\w*View\w*)\s*\(/g;
```

Real SwiftUI apps frequently use names like `ProductDetail`, `OnboardingScreen`, `CheckoutFlow`. None of those would be detected. This is a significant false-negative scenario that should at minimum be documented in the module or in a follow-up issue.

#### 🟡 `findEnclosingSwiftView` is a best-effort heuristic

```typescript
// swiftui-navigation.ts lines 24–31
const findEnclosingSwiftView = (content: string, offset: number): string | undefined => {
  const before = content.slice(0, offset);
  const structRe = /struct\s+(\w+)\s*(?::\s*[\w,\s]+)?\{/g;
  let lastMatch: string | undefined;
  while ((m = structRe.exec(before)) !== null) { lastMatch = m[1]; }
  return lastMatch;
};
```

This returns the **last struct declaration before the match**, not the truly enclosing struct. For a file with two structs where the second struct contains a `NavigationLink`, if the first struct appears earlier in the file, this could misattribute the source. It works for simple single-struct files (like the fixtures) but is fragile for multi-struct files without brace balancing.

---

#### 🟡 `TABVIEW_RE` requires a newline before `}`

```typescript
const TABVIEW_RE = /TabView\s*(?:\([^)]*\))?\s*\{([\s\S]*?)\n\}/g;
```

The `\n\}` anchor means TabViews where the closing `}` has different whitespace or is on the same line will be silently missed. Prefer `\s*\}` or a brace-balancing approach.

### 🔴 New #A — CALL/CANCEL/CICS/ENTRY Edge Source Always Uses Outer Program's Module (`parentId`)

`cobol-processor.ts:537–544`, `:521–528`, `:644`, `:677`, `:792`:

```typescript
const parentId = moduleId ?? fileNodeId;  // line 361 — outer program's module, NEVER updated

// CALL (line 537):
graph.addRelationship({ ..., sourceId: parentId, reason: 'cobol-call' });

// Dynamic CALL CONTAINS (line 521):
graph.addRelationship({ ..., sourceId: parentId, reason: 'cobol-dynamic-call' });

// CICS LINK/XCTL (line 677):
graph.addRelationship({ ..., sourceId: parentId, ... });

// ENTRY CONTAINS (line 792):
graph.addRelationship({ ..., sourceId: parentId, reason: 'cobol-entry-point' });

// CANCEL (line 945):
graph.addRelationship({ ..., sourceId: parentId, reason: 'cobol-cancel' });
```

In the 8th review, `CONTAINS` edges for sections, paragraphs, and data items were corrected to use `programModuleIds.get(owningPgm ?? '') ?? parentId`. However, this fix was not applied to CALLS/ACCESSES edges from cross-program constructs: CALL, dynamic CALL, CICS LINK/XCTL, CICS RETURN/START, ENTRY, and CANCEL.

For files with nested programs, all CALL, CICS LINK, and CANCEL edges in inner programs are incorrectly attributed to the outer program's Module node. A query like "show me all programs called by INNER-PGM" returns nothing; instead, OUTER-PGM appears to be the caller.

**Note:** PERFORM, MOVE, and GO TO are correctly handled because they use `scopedCallerLookup(caller, line)` which resolves to the paragraph node. The gap is specifically in constructs that use `parentId` directly as source.

Fix: For each affected construct, compute `findOwningProgramName(line, extracted.programs)` and use `programModuleIds.get(owningPgm ?? '') ?? parentId` as sourceId.

`cobol-processor.ts:465–469`:


### 🟢 New #E — `pendingProcUsing` Set to `true` for `PROCEDURE DIVISION.` (Period-Terminated, No USING)

`cobol-preprocessor.ts:904–907`:

```typescript
} else {
  // USING may be on the next line — flag for extractProcedure to pick up
  pendingProcUsing = true;
}
```

When a nested inner program declares `PROCEDURE DIVISION.` (period on same line, no USING), `RE_PROC_USING` fails to match and the `else` branch sets `pendingProcUsing = true`. The intent is to handle `PROCEDURE DIVISION\n    USING params.` (split-line), but a period-terminated declaration has no USING to expect.

The impact is low: `extractProcedure` clears `pendingProcUsing = false` on the first inner procedure line. If that line matches a USING pattern (unlikely in procedure body), it would spuriously populate `result.procedureUsing`. If it doesn't match USING, the line is still processed normally (the early return at line 1187 only fires when `usingMatch` succeeds).

Fix: Only set `pendingProcUsing = true` when the line does NOT end with a period:
```typescript
if (!/\.\s*$/.test(line)) pendingProcUsing = true;
```

## New Findings (This Review)

### 🔴 New #1 — `scopedCallerLookup(null, lineNum)` Returns Outer `parentId` for Nested Programs

`cobol-processor.ts:465–469`:

```typescript
const scopedCallerLookup = (name: string | null, lineNum: number): string => {
  if (!name) return parentId;   // ← BUG: should be owningModuleId(lineNum)
  const pgm = findOwningProgramName(lineNum, extracted.programs);
  return paraNodeIds.get(`${pgm ?? ''}:${name.toUpperCase()}`)
    ?? (programModuleIds.get(pgm ?? '') ?? parentId);
};
```

The 9th review's fix for finding #D correctly updated the non-null branch to use `programModuleIds.get(pgm ?? '') ?? parentId`. However, the **null guard** (`if (!name) return parentId`) was not updated. This is used when `currentParagraph` is null — i.e., when procedure-level statements appear before the program's first paragraph.

For a nested program that has PERFORM/MOVE/GOTO before its first paragraph:

```cobol
PROGRAM-ID. INNER-PROG.
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    PERFORM INNER-INIT.   ← currentParagraph = null, lineNum inside INNER-PROG
INNER-INIT.
    ...
END PROGRAM INNER-PROG.
```

`scopedCallerLookup(null, lineNum)` returns `parentId` (outer program's module) instead of `owningModuleId(lineNum)` (inner program's module). The PERFORM edge from `INNER-PROG`'s top-level code is incorrectly attributed to `OUTER-PROG`.

Note: CALL/CANCEL/CICS all use `owningModuleId(lineNum)` directly and are **not** affected. Only PERFORM, MOVE, and GO TO (which route through `scopedCallerLookup`) have this gap.

Fix: `if (!name) return owningModuleId(lineNum);`

[Fix this →](https://claude.ai/code?q=In%20gitnexus%2Fsrc%2Fcore%2Fingestion%2Fcobol-processor.ts%20on%20branch%20feat%2Fcobol-language-support%2C%20fix%20scopedCallerLookup%20at%20line%20466.%20Change%20%60if%20%28!name%29%20return%20parentId%3B%60%20to%20%60if%20%28!name%29%20return%20owningModuleId%28lineNum%29%3B%60.%20This%20ensures%20that%20PERFORM%2FMOVE%2FGOTO%20statements%20before%20the%20first%20paragraph%20in%20a%20nested%20program%20are%20attributed%20to%20the%20nested%20program%27s%20module%2C%20not%20the%20outer%20program%27s%20module.%20CALL%2FCANCEL%2FCICS%20already%20use%20owningModuleId%28%29%20directly%20and%20are%20not%20affected.)

### 🟡 New #2 — Multiple CALL Statements on the Same Logical Line: Only First Captured

`cobol-preprocessor.ts:944–954`:

```typescript
const callMatch = line.match(RE_CALL);
if (callMatch) {
  result.calls.push({ target: callMatch[1] ?? callMatch[2], line: lineNum, isQuoted: true });
} else {   // ← only checks dynamic if NO quoted match
  const dynCallMatch = line.match(RE_CALL_DYNAMIC);
  ...
}
```

`RE_CALL` uses `.match()` (no `g` flag) — only the first quoted CALL is captured. The `else` branch also prevents dynamic CALL detection on any line that contains a quoted CALL.

For COBOL programs that use inline exception handling:

```cobol
       CALL 'MAINPROG' ON EXCEPTION CALL WS-FALLBACK-PGM.
```

Only `MAINPROG` is captured. `WS-FALLBACK-PGM` (a dynamic CALL in the ON EXCEPTION clause) is invisible. For programs with rich error-handling logic using CALL ON OVERFLOW, CALL ON EXCEPTION, or chained CALLs in conditional expressions, secondary CALLs are systematically missed.

Fix: replace the single `match()` call with a `matchAll()` scan for quoted CALLs, and separately run `RE_CALL_DYNAMIC` against the remaining text (excluding quoted-match spans).

[Fix this →](https://claude.ai/code?q=In%20gitnexus%2Fsrc%2Fcore%2Fingestion%2Fcobol%2Fcobol-preprocessor.ts%20on%20branch%20feat%2Fcobol-language-support%20at%20lines%20944-954%20in%20processLogicalLine%2C%20fix%20CALL%20extraction%20to%20capture%20all%20quoted%20CALLs%20on%20a%20line%20and%20also%20check%20for%20dynamic%20CALLs%20even%20when%20a%20quoted%20CALL%20was%20found.%20Use%20RE_CALL%20with%20a%20global%20flag%20%28matchAll%29%20to%20iterate%20all%20quoted%20matches%2C%20then%20also%20check%20RE_CALL_DYNAMIC%20separately.%20The%20current%20if%2Felse%20structure%20means%20dynamic%20CALL%20is%20never%20checked%20on%20lines%20that%20also%20have%20a%20quoted%20CALL.)

### 🟡 New #4 — SORT/MERGE ACCESSES Edge ID Uses `parentId` (Outer Module) Not `owningModuleId`

`cobol-processor.ts:895–913`:

```typescript
for (const usingFile of sort.usingFiles) {
  graph.addRelationship({
    id: generateId('ACCESSES', `${parentId}->sort-using->${usingFile}:L${sort.line}`), // ← parentId
    type: 'ACCESSES',
    sourceId: sortFileId,  // ← sortFileId (Record node), not module
    ...
  });
}
```

The edge ID uses `parentId` (outer module's ID) for all SORT edges regardless of which program contains the SORT statement. The actual `sourceId` is `sortFileId` (a Record node — the sort work file), which is correct semantically. But the ID generation uses `parentId`, so for a nested program that runs a SORT, the edge ID would reference the outer module's ID. This creates:

1. **Incorrect edge IDs** for SORT edges in nested programs (minor — no collision since line numbers are unique per file)
2. **Missing sort-file CONTAINS edge** — `sortFileId` is generated as a Record node ID, but `graph.addNode` is never called for it here. The node only exists if the sort file was also declared in the ENVIRONMENT DIVISION SELECT. For standard COBOL this is always true, but a defensive `graph.addNode` call would be more robust.

[Fix this →](https://claude.ai/code?q=In%20gitnexus%2Fsrc%2Fcore%2Fingestion%2Fcobol-processor.ts%20on%20branch%20feat%2Fcobol-language-support%20at%20lines%20895-913%2C%20fix%20SORT%2FMERGE%20ACCESSES%20edge%20ID%20to%20use%20owningModuleId%28sort.line%29%20instead%20of%20parentId%20in%20the%20generateId%20call.%20Also%20consider%20whether%20a%20defensive%20graph.addNode%20should%20be%20called%20for%20sortFileId%20to%20handle%20cases%20where%20the%20sort%20file%20has%20no%20SELECT%20statement.)

### 🟢 New #5 — `preprocessCobolSource` and `extractCobolSymbolsWithRegex` Have Inconsistent Free-Format Detection Thresholds

`preprocessCobolSource` (line 138): checks `content.substring(0, 500)` (first 500 characters)  
`extractCobolSymbolsWithRegex` (line 678): checks `rawLines[0..9]` (first 10 lines)

For a file where `>>SOURCE FREE` appears in line 5, with 4 lines of 125 characters each (= exactly 500 chars before line 5): `preprocessCobolSource` would return the content unchanged (correctly). But for files where `>>SOURCE FREE` is in line 4–10 with longer preceding lines, `preprocessCobolSource` might NOT detect the directive (scanning only 500 chars) while `extractCobolSymbolsWithRegex` DOES detect it (scanning first 10 lines). In that case, `preprocessCobolSource` would blank cols 1-6 of the free-format source (incorrectly), then `extractCobolSymbolsWithRegex` would treat it as free-format but the content has already been corrupted.

Fix: use the same threshold in both functions, or pass the `isFreeFormat` flag from one to the other.

### 🟢 New #6 — `RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH` False-Positive on Isolated COBOL Verbs with Trailing Periods

`cobol-preprocessor.ts:209`:
```typescript
const RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH = /^\s*([A-Z][A-Z0-9-]+)\.\s*$/i;
```

COBOL verbs that appear alone on a line terminated by a period (unusual but valid in some dialects or malformed source) would create spurious Function nodes:

- `DISPLAY.` — not in `EXCLUDED_PARA_NAMES`
- `ACCEPT.` — not in `EXCLUDED_PARA_NAMES`  
- `WRITE.` — not in `EXCLUDED_PARA_NAMES`
- `READ.` — not in `EXCLUDED_PARA_NAMES`

`GOBACK.`, `STOP.`, `EXIT.`, `CONTINUE.` are correctly excluded. High-frequency verbs like `DISPLAY`, `ACCEPT`, `WRITE`, `READ` are not. For malformed or unusual COBOL source (which is common in legacy mainframe repositories), these could produce spurious paragraph nodes.

A more complete `EXCLUDED_PARA_NAMES` set would reduce this noise. Low impact for well-formed COBOL.

### 🟡 New #3 — `RE_CALL_DYNAMIC` Trailing `(?:\s|\.)` Drops Dynamic CALLs as Last Token on Line

`cobol-preprocessor.ts:276`:

```typescript
const RE_CALL_DYNAMIC = /(?<![A-Z0-9-])\bCALL\s+([A-Z][A-Z0-9-]+)(?:\s|\.)/gi;
```

The `(?:\s|\.)` anchor requires the captured identifier to be followed by a space or period. When a dynamic CALL is the last physical-line token (common in multi-line call statements without continuation markers), the match fails:

```cobol
       CALL WS-PROGRAM
           USING WS-DATA.
```

In fixed-format COBOL, the preprocessor treats each physical line as a separate logical line (only `−` in col 7 creates explicit continuations). Line 1 (`CALL WS-PROGRAM`) — the identifier `WS-PROGRAM` is at end of string with no trailing character. Match fails → the call is completely missed.

Fix: change `(?:\s|\.)` to `(?=\s|\.|$)` (lookahead) or `(?:\s|\.|$)` (non-consuming), allowing end-of-line.

[Fix this →](https://claude.ai/code?q=In%20gitnexus%2Fsrc%2Fcore%2Fingestion%2Fcobol%2Fcobol-preprocessor.ts%20on%20branch%20feat%2Fcobol-language-support%2C%20fix%20RE_CALL_DYNAMIC%20at%20line%20276%20to%20allow%20matching%20when%20the%20dynamic%20CALL%20identifier%20is%20the%20last%20token%20on%20the%20physical%20line.%20Change%20%60%28%3F%3A%5Cs%7C%5C.%29%60%20to%20%60%28%3F%3D%5Cs%7C%5C.%7C%24%29%60%20%28lookahead%2C%20non-consuming%29.%20The%20current%20pattern%20drops%20dynamic%20CALLs%20in%20multi-line%20CALL%20statements%20where%20CALL%20WS-PROGRAM%20appears%20on%20one%20line%20and%20USING%20parameters%20on%20the%20next.)

### 🟡 New #4 — Multi-Line CALL USING Parameters on Separate Physical Lines Are Silently Lost

When a CALL USING clause spans multiple physical lines without explicit continuation markers, only parameters on the same physical line as CALL are captured:

```cobol
       CALL 'SUBPROG'
           USING BY REFERENCE WS-INPUT-REC
                              WS-OUTPUT-REC
                              WS-CONTROL-REC.
```

Each physical line is processed as a separate logical line (the preprocessor only merges lines with `−` in col 7). Line 1 (`CALL 'SUBPROG'`) — CALL captured, no USING. Lines 2–4 — standalone `USING`/identifier lines don't match any pattern in `extractProcedure`. Result: the CALL structural edge exists, but all three `cobol-call-using` ACCESSES edges are silently lost.

This is one of the most common COBOL coding styles in IBM mainframe codebases — parameters on separate indented lines with no continuation markers. All ACCESSES parameter data-flow edges are missing for such calls.

Fix: add a CALL accumulator (parallel to `sortAccum`/`selectAccum`) — start accumulating when `RE_CALL` fires on a non-period-terminated line, continue until period, then extract USING from the full statement.

[Fix this →](https://claude.ai/code?q=In%20gitnexus%2Fsrc%2Fcore%2Fingestion%2Fcobol%2Fcobol-preprocessor.ts%20on%20branch%20feat%2Fcobol-language-support%2C%20add%20a%20CALL%20statement%20accumulator%20for%20multi-line%20CALL%20USING%20parsing.%20Follow%20the%20sortAccum%20%2F%20selectAccum%20pattern%3A%20when%20RE_CALL%20or%20RE_CALL_DYNAMIC%20fires%20and%20the%20logical%20line%20does%20not%20end%20with%20a%20period%2C%20set%20%60callAccum%20%3D%20line%60%20and%20return.%20On%20subsequent%20lines%20while%20callAccum%20is%20active%2C%20append%20and%20check%20for%20period.%20When%20period%20is%20found%2C%20re-extract%20USING%20parameters%20from%20the%20full%20accumulated%20statement.%20This%20fixes%20the%20silent%20loss%20of%20ACCESSES%20parameter%20edges%20when%20USING%20appears%20on%20lines%20after%20the%20CALL.)

### 🟢 New #6 — SORT Accumulation: Period-Terminated Continuation Line Also Starting a New SORT Drops the New SORT

`cobol-preprocessor.ts:1573–1587`:


### 🔴 New #2 — `flushCallAccum` USING Extraction Too Broad: Absorbs Adjacent COBOL Statements

`cobol-preprocessor.ts:1346`:

```typescript
const usingMatch = afterCall.match(
  /\bUSING\s+([\s\S]*?)(?=\bRETURNING\b|\bON\s+(?:EXCEPTION|OVERFLOW)\b|\bNOT\s+ON\b|\bEND-CALL\b|\.\s*$|$)/i
);
```

The lazy `[\s\S]*?` stops only at RETURNING, ON EXCEPTION, END-CALL, or the terminating period. When a CALL without `END-CALL` is followed by an INSPECT/SORT/DISPLAY and the terminating period is on that next statement's line, the statement keywords are absorbed as CALL USING parameters:

```cobol
       CALL 'CUSTUPDT'
           USING WS-PARM
       INSPECT WS-STATUS TALLYING WS-CNT FOR ALL SPACES.
```

`callAccum` accumulates until the period on the INSPECT line. `flushCallAccum()` runs on:
`"CALL 'CUSTUPDT' USING WS-PARM INSPECT WS-STATUS TALLYING WS-CNT FOR ALL SPACES."`

The USING extraction's lazy match captures `WS-PARM INSPECT WS-STATUS TALLYING WS-CNT FOR ALL SPACES` (stopping before the terminating period). After filtering through `CALL_USING_FILTER` and identifier regex:
- `WS-PARM` ✓ (correct parameter)
- `INSPECT`, `WS-STATUS`, `TALLYING`, `WS-CNT`, `FOR`, `ALL`, `SPACES` — all pass the identifier regex and are not in `CALL_USING_FILTER`

Real data items named `WS-STATUS` and `WS-CNT` receive false `cobol-call-using` ACCESSES edges. Impact: corrupted data-flow attribution for calls followed by statement-level constructs without `END-CALL`.

The affected case is COBOL programs written in pre-COBOL-85 style without scope terminators (common in IBM legacy code). Adding `END-CALL` was introduced in COBOL-85 but is not universal in legacy codebases.

Fix: add common statement boundaries to the lookahead:

```typescript
/\bUSING\s+([\s\S]*?)(?=\bRETURNING\b|\bON\s+(?:EXCEPTION|OVERFLOW)\b|\bNOT\s+ON\b|\bEND-CALL\b|\bINSPECT\b|\bSEARCH\b|\bSORT\b|\bMERGE\b|\bDISPLAY\b|\bACCEPT\b|\bMOVE\b|\bPERFORM\b|\bGO\s+TO\b|\.\s*$|$)/i
```

[Fix this →](https://claude.ai/code?q=In%20gitnexus%2Fsrc%2Fcore%2Fingestion%2Fcobol%2Fcobol-preprocessor.ts%20on%20branch%20feat%2Fcobol-language-support%20at%20line%201346%2C%20fix%20the%20USING%20extraction%20regex%20in%20flushCallAccum%20to%20stop%20before%20common%20COBOL%20statement%20verbs.%20The%20current%20lazy%20match%20only%20stops%20at%20RETURNING%2C%20ON%20EXCEPTION%2C%20END-CALL%2C%20and%20period.%20Add%20%5CbINSPECT%5Cb%2C%20%5CbSEARCH%5Cb%2C%20%5CbSORT%5Cb%2C%20%5CbMERGE%5Cb%2C%20%5CbDISPLAY%5Cb%2C%20%5CbACCEPT%5Cb%2C%20%5CbMOVE%5Cb%2C%20%5CbPERFORM%5Cb%2C%20%5CbGO%5Cs%2BTO%5Cb%20as%20additional%20lookahead%20alternatives.%20Without%20this%2C%20a%20CALL%20without%20END-CALL%20whose%20period%20is%20on%20the%20INSPECT%20or%20SORT%20line%20gets%20those%20statement%20keywords%20captured%20as%20false%20USING%20parameters.)

### 🟡 New #3 — CICS FILE Record Nodes Are File-Path-Scoped (Inconsistent With SQL Tables)

`cobol-processor.ts:818`:

```typescript
const fileRecordId = generateId('Record', `${filePath}:${cics.fileName}`);
```

SQL table nodes at line 702 use a globally-scoped key:
```typescript
const tableId = generateId('Record', `<db>:${table}`);
```

CICS files use a per-file-scoped key. Two programs that both access the same VSAM dataset through CICS (e.g., `FILE('CUSTOMER')`) receive **different** Record nodes:
- `CUSTUPDT.cbl:CUSTOMER` → Record node A
- `RPTGEN.cbl:CUSTOMER` → Record node B

No relationship between A and B exists in the graph, even though they represent the same VSAM dataset. Cross-program CICS file access analysis is impossible — a query like "which programs access the CUSTOMER VSAM file?" would return each program independently with no shared resource node to pivot on.

Fix: use a globally-scoped key consistent with SQL tables:

```typescript
const fileRecordId = generateId('Record', `<cics-file>:${cics.fileName.toUpperCase()}`);
```

Note: the `.toUpperCase()` ensures `FILE('Customer')` and `FILE('CUSTOMER')` map to the same node (CICS file names are case-insensitive in resource definitions).

[Fix this →](https://claude.ai/code?q=In%20gitnexus%2Fsrc%2Fcore%2Fingestion%2Fcobol-processor.ts%20on%20branch%20feat%2Fcobol-language-support%20at%20line%20818%2C%20fix%20CICS%20FILE%20Record%20node%20scoping%20to%20be%20globally-scoped%20like%20SQL%20table%20nodes.%20Change%20%60generateId%28%27Record%27%2C%20%60%24%7BfilePath%7D%3A%24%7Bcics.fileName%7D%60%29%60%20to%20%60generateId%28%27Record%27%2C%20%60%3Ccics-file%3E%3A%24%7Bcics.fileName.toUpperCase%28%29%7D%60%29%60.%20SQL%20tables%20use%20%60%3Cdb%3E%3Atable%60%20for%20global%20scoping%3B%20CICS%20files%20should%20use%20%60%3Ccics-file%3E%3AFILENAME%60%20so%20that%20multiple%20programs%20accessing%20the%20same%20VSAM%20file%20share%20one%20Record%20node.)

### 🔴 New #1 — `callAccum` Flush Triggers False Paragraph Detection + `currentParagraph` Corruption

`cobol-preprocessor.ts:1148–1153` and `cobol-preprocessor.ts:1525–1532`:

```typescript
// Line 1148-1153: callAccum flush (no return)
if (callAccum !== null) {
  callAccum += ' ' + line;
  if (/\.\s*$/.test(callAccum) || /\bEND-CALL\b/i.test(callAccum)) {
    flushCallAccum();
  }
  // Don't return — line may contain other extractable constructs after the period
}
// ... switch(currentDivision) → case 'procedure': → line 1525
const paraMatch = line.match(RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH);  // RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH = /^\s*([A-Z][A-Z0-9-]+)\.\s*$/i
if (paraMatch) {
  const name = paraMatch[1];
  if (!EXCLUDED_PARA_NAMES.has(name.toUpperCase()) && ...) {
    result.paragraphs.push({ name, line: lineNum });
    currentParagraph = name;   // ← SET TO DATA-ITEM NAME!
  }
  return;
}
```

**Scenario** (extremely common in IBM mainframe COBOL):
```cobol
       CALL 'CUSTPRC'
           USING BY REFERENCE WS-CUST-ID
                              WS-CUST-NAME
                              WS-CUST-ADDR.   ← last param alone on line
       PERFORM VALIDATE-DATA.
       PERFORM WRITE-OUTPUT.
   CALC-SECTION.
       ...
```

When `                              WS-CUST-ADDR.` is processed:
1. callAccum appends it and finds the period → `flushCallAccum()` correctly extracts parameters
2. No `return` — code falls through to `switch (currentDivision)`
3. `case 'procedure':` → `RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH = /^\s*([A-Z][A-Z0-9-]+)\.\s*$/i` **matches** `WS-CUST-ADDR.`
4. `WS-CUST-ADDR` is not in `EXCLUDED_PARA_NAMES` → `result.paragraphs.push(...)` **false paragraph created**
5. `currentParagraph = 'WS-CUST-ADDR'` **state corrupted**
6. `return` exits — PERFORM/MOVE/CALL below are attributed to `WS-CUST-ADDR` until `CALC-SECTION.`

**Impact**: Every multi-line CALL USING with its last parameter alone on a period-terminated line creates a spurious Function node named after a data item. More critically, `currentParagraph` is set to the data item name, causing all subsequent PERFORM/MOVE/CALL/GOTO edges (until the next real paragraph) to be attributed to the false paragraph node. The call graph becomes structurally incorrect between the false paragraph and the next real one.

This pattern is ubiquitous in IBM COBOL — programs with 3+ USING parameters almost universally put each one on its own line, and the last one ends with the statement period.

**Fix**: Track that `callAccum` was flushed on the current line and skip paragraph detection for that line:

```typescript
let callAccumFlushedThisLine = false;
if (callAccum !== null) {
  callAccum += ' ' + line;
  if (/\.\s*$/.test(callAccum) || /\bEND-CALL\b/i.test(callAccum)) {
    flushCallAccum();
    callAccumFlushedThisLine = true;
  }
}
// ... later in case 'procedure':
if (!callAccumFlushedThisLine) {
  const paraMatch = line.match(RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH);
  ...
}
```

### 🟢 New #5 — `RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH` Has No Protection Against Deep-Indented DATA DIVISION Continuations

As a follow-on to New #1, the broader pattern is: `RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH = /^\s*([A-Z][A-Z0-9-]+)\.\s*$/i` uses `^\s*` (zero or more spaces) rather than anchoring to Area A (col 8–11 in fixed format). In fixed-format COBOL, paragraph names must appear in Area A (columns 8–11), meaning 7 spaces of leading whitespace. Data items in Area B (columns 12+) have more than 7 spaces.

Adding a column-position check would eliminate false-positive paragraph matches for any identifier at Area B indentation. This is a systemic guard that would prevent similar future regressions:

```typescript
// Only accept paragraph headers if identifier starts in Area A (col 8-11, i.e. 7 leading spaces max)
// Area B indentation (8+ leading spaces) is for statements, not paragraph headers
const RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH = /^\s{0,7}([A-Z][A-Z0-9-]+)\.\s*$/i;
```

Note: this would only apply in fixed-format mode. Free-format COBOL has no column restrictions.

### 🔴 New #A — Last CALL USING Parameter Dropped When on Its Own Period-Terminated Line; False Paragraph in Free-Format Mode

`cobol-preprocessor.ts:1154–1157`:

```typescript
if (/^(?:GO\s+TO|PERFORM|MOVE|...|START)\b/i.test(trimmedLine)
  || RE_PROC_SECTION.test(line) || RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH.test(line)) {
  flushCallAccum(); // Flush CALL without this line's content

```

The fix for 14th review New #1 introduced this regression. When `callAccum !== null` and the line matches `RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH = /^\s*([A-Z][A-Z0-9-]+)\.\s*$/i` — which includes ANY line consisting of a single identifier + period — `flushCallAccum()` is called **without the current line**. In the dominant IBM mainframe coding style where the last USING parameter appears alone on a period-terminated line, it is silently dropped:

```cobol
       CALL 'CUSTUPDT'
           USING BY REFERENCE WS-CUST-ID
                              WS-CUST-NAME
                              WS-CUST-ADDR.    ← RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH matches
```

**Fixed-format mode:** `WS-CUST-ADDR.` has many leading spaces (Area B). Early flush fires WITHOUT `WS-CUST-ADDR`. Falls through to `extractProcedure` where the Area A guard rejects it as a paragraph. Result: **`WS-CUST-ADDR` silently dropped from CALL parameters — missing `cobol-call-using` ACCESSES edge**.

**Free-format mode (GnuCOBOL / ACAS benchmark — 268 programs):** Same early flush, but `isFreeFormat = true` means the Area A guard at line 1543 is **disabled**. `WS-CUST-ADDR` is created as a false paragraph, `currentParagraph = 'WS-CUST-ADDR'` — all subsequent PERFORM/MOVE/CALL edges until the next real paragraph are misattributed to the spurious node. The original problem from the 14th review reappears, unchanged, in free-format mode.

**Root cause:** `RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH` cannot distinguish between an Area B USING parameter `                 WS-ADDR.` and an Area A paragraph header `       NEXT-PARA.` without considering column position. The 14th review fix applies the Area A check in `extractProcedure` (after the early flush), not inside the callAccum decision block where it is needed.

**Fix:** Apply the Area A constraint inside the callAccum flush-trigger decision. In fixed-format, only use `RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH` as a flush trigger when the line is in Area A (≤7 leading spaces). In free-format, never use `RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH` as a flush trigger (rely only on statement verbs and `RE_PROC_SECTION`):

```typescript
const matchesPara = RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH.test(line);
const leadingSpaces = (line.match(/^(\s*)/)?.[1].length ?? 0);
// Fixed-format: only flush for Area A para headers (≤7 spaces). Area B = USING param.
// Free-format: never flush for RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH (no column semantics).
const isParaFlushTrigger = !isFreeFormat && matchesPara && leadingSpaces <= 7;
if (statementVerbMatch || RE_PROC_SECTION.test(line) || isParaFlushTrigger) {
  flushCallAccum();
  // Fall through to process this line normally
} else {
  callAccum += ' ' + line;
  if (/\.\s*$/.test(callAccum) || /\bEND-CALL\b/i.test(callAccum)) {
    flushCallAccum();
  }
  return;
}
```

This correctly accumulates Area B USING parameters (fixed-format) or any period-terminated parameter line (free-format via the period trigger), while still detecting Area A paragraph headers as a flush signal.

### 🟢 New #D — Free-Format CALL USING Last Parameter: No Correct Termination Signal

In free-format mode (`isFreeFormat = true`), the proposed fix for New #A (not using `RE_PROC_PARAGRAPH` as a flush trigger) means the only flush triggers are: statement verbs, `RE_PROC_SECTION`, and the period in the accumulated text. For:

```cobol

              WS-PARAM-B
```

`WS-PARAM-C.` is appended to `callAccum`, period found → `flushCallAccum()` with all three params. ✓

However, for free-format with no `END-CALL` and no period on the last parameter line (which is non-standard but possible in truncated/malformed source), `callAccum` would accumulate indefinitely until the next period-terminated line. This is the same behavior as any other non-period-terminated CALL and is handled by the EOF flush at line 959.

This is a design note, not a bug — just worth confirming the fix for New #A doesn't introduce a free-format regression.

Added integration tests for Dart field-type resolution and call-result binding, along with five pipeline fixes to make them pass.

### What's fixed

### 🔴 Finding 1 — `END PROGRAM` does not flush `callAccum` (HIGH)

**Location:** `cobol-preprocessor.ts` lines 1078–1093

```typescript
const endProgramMatch = line.match(RE_END_PROGRAM);
if (endProgramMatch) {
  const topProgram = programBoundaryStack.pop();
  // ... push to result.programs ...
  return;   // ← callAccum NOT flushed
}
```

**Impact:** If a multi-line `CALL` statement is left open at the end of Program A's procedure division and `END PROGRAM PROG-A.` is the next structural line, `callAccum` silently carries live state across the program boundary. The accumulated text from Program A is then either:

- Flushed during Program B's first matching flush trigger (wrong owning program, wrong `callAccumLine`), or
- Silently dropped if Program B has no subsequent flush trigger before the file ends.

**Concrete trigger:**
```cobol
       CALL 'PROG-A-SUB' USING WS-DATA       ← no period, no END-CALL
       END PROGRAM OUTER.                     ← returns without flush
       PROGRAM-ID. INNER.                     ← flush still pending
```

**Fix:** Call `flushCallAccum(); flushSort(); flushInspect();` before the `return` in the `endProgramMatch` block — identical to the division-boundary flush at lines 1119–1122.

---

### 🔴 Finding 2 — `PROGRAM-ID` detection path does not flush `callAccum` (HIGH)

**Location:** `cobol-preprocessor.ts` lines 1107–1113

```typescript
if (currentDivision !== 'identification') {
  const pgmIdMatch = line.match(RE_PROGRAM_ID);
  if (pgmIdMatch) {
    extractIdentification(line, lineNum);
    return;   // ← callAccum NOT flushed
  }
}
```

This path is reached for sibling programs whose `IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.` header is omitted (common in COBOL source that uses abbreviated structure after `END PROGRAM`). The comment at line 1105 confirms this intent.

**Impact:** Compounds Finding 1. Even when `END PROGRAM` is present, if the next non-blank line is `PROGRAM-ID.` rather than `IDENTIFICATION DIVISION.`, callAccum is still not flushed at this second-chance boundary. The accumulated CALL text from Program A gets attributed to Program B via `callAccumLine` which still points into Program A's line range.

**Fix:** Same as Finding 1 — add flush calls before `return` here.

---

### 🟡 Finding 3 — Arithmetic verbs absent from `COBOL_STATEMENT_VERBS` (MEDIUM)

**Location:** `cobol-preprocessor.ts` lines 377–398

```typescript
const COBOL_STATEMENT_VERBS = [
  'GO\\s+TO', 'PERFORM', 'MOVE', 'DISPLAY', 'ACCEPT',
  'INSPECT', 'SEARCH', 'SORT', 'MERGE', 'IF', 'EVALUATE',
  'SET', 'INITIALIZE', 'STOP', 'EXIT', 'GOBACK', 'CONTINUE',
  'READ', 'WRITE', 'REWRITE', 'DELETE', 'OPEN', 'CLOSE', 'START',
  'CANCEL',
  // ← COMPUTE, ADD, SUBTRACT, MULTIPLY, DIVIDE, STRING, UNSTRING absent
];
```

**Impact:** A multi-line `CALL` with an arithmetic continuation (pre-COBOL-85 implicit termination via the next statement's period) is not flushed when the arithmetic line is encountered. Instead the arithmetic line is appended to `callAccum`. When the period on the arithmetic line triggers `flushCallAccum()`, `RE_USING_PARAMS` scans the combined text and extracts identifiers from the arithmetic line as false USING parameters:

```cobol
       CALL 'PAYROLL' USING WS-RATE WS-HOURS
       COMPUTE WS-TOTAL = WS-RATE * WS-HOURS.
```

After accumulation, `flushCallAccum` sees:
```
CALL 'PAYROLL' USING WS-RATE WS-HOURS COMPUTE WS-TOTAL = WS-RATE * WS-HOURS.
```

`RE_USING_PARAMS` stops at `\.` (period) and the `CALL_USING_FILTER` does not contain `COMPUTE` or `WS-TOTAL`. The identifier filter `/^[A-Z][A-Z0-9-]+$/i` matches `COMPUTE` and `WS-TOTAL`, injecting them as phantom parameters.

**Affected verbs to add:** `COMPUTE`, `ADD`, `SUBTRACT`, `MULTIPLY`, `DIVIDE`, `STRING`, `UNSTRING` — all are COBOL statement-opening verbs that cannot legally appear within a CALL's USING clause.

**Fix:** Add these seven verbs to `COBOL_STATEMENT_VERBS`. They will automatically propagate into `RE_STATEMENT_VERB_START` (callAccum / inspectAccum flush trigger) and `USING_VERB_LOOKAHEAD` (RE_USING_PARAMS terminator), closing both the flush gap and the false-parameter extraction gap simultaneously.

---

### 🟢 Finding 4 — Section `endLine` crosses nested program boundaries (LOW / cosmetic)

**Location:** `cobol-processor.ts` lines 392–394 (same as 16th review finding #5 — still present)

```typescript
const nextLine = sections[i + 1]?.line - 1 ?? fileLines;
```

Section `i` and section `i+1` may belong to different nested programs. `endLine` is over-extended across the program boundary, producing a wider line range than the true section scope. This does not affect correctness of edges (owning module is resolved by `owningModuleId()` / `findOwningProgramName()`), but makes Namespace node metadata misleading in the graph output.

### 🔬 New Findings — 20th Review

#### Finding 1 — `RE_INITIALIZE` captures only the first target identifier 🟡 MEDIUM

**Location:** `cobol-preprocessor.ts` line 313  
**Pattern:** `RE_INITIALIZE = /\bINITIALIZE\s+([A-Z][A-Z0-9-]+)/i`

The regex captures exactly one identifier after `INITIALIZE`. In standard COBOL, `INITIALIZE` accepts a space-separated list of targets:

```cobol
INITIALIZE WS-CUSTOMER WS-ORDER WS-LINE-ITEM.
```

With the current pattern, only `WS-CUSTOMER` produces an ACCESSES write edge. `WS-ORDER` and `WS-LINE-ITEM` are silently dropped — meaning the data-flow graph is incomplete for any multi-target `INITIALIZE`.

**Fix:** Replace the single-capture regex with a `matchAll` loop over token positions, or capture the full tail and split on whitespace (filtering out `WITH`, `REPLACING`, `ALL`, `ALPHABETIC`, `NUMERIC`, etc. which are INITIALIZE clause keywords):

```typescript
RE_INITIALIZE_TAIL = /\bINITIALIZE\s+((?:[A-Z][A-Z0-9-]+\s*)+)/i
// then: tail.match(/[A-Z][A-Z0-9-]+/gi)?.filter(t => !INITIALIZE_CLAUSE_KEYWORDS.has(t))
```

This is the same `matchAll` pattern already used for CALL/CANCEL extraction and is consistent with the rest of the pipeline.

---

#### Finding 2 — COPY detection runs before `callAccum` continuation guard 🟢 LOW

**Location:** `cobol-preprocessor.ts` lines 1179–1193 (`processLogicalLine`)

The COPY detection block executes unconditionally before the `callAccum` block. In formally valid COBOL a COPY statement cannot appear mid-CALL; however a source file with a malformed or concatenated COPY inside a CALL argument list (e.g. a source generator artefact) would:

1. Push a spurious entry to `result.copies`
2. Skip the `callAccum` continuation, silently abandoning the in-progress CALL

This is an edge case for invalid source only, but a static analyser operating on real-world legacy codebases (which frequently contain pre-processor noise) will encounter it. **No action required for MVP**, but worth a defensive `if (callAccum) { flushCallAccum(); }` before the COPY push if robustness against malformed input is ever needed.

---

#### Finding 3 — Single-line CALL + active `sortAccum` contamination 🟢 LOW

**Location:** `cobol-preprocessor.ts` lines 1213–1225 (single-line CALL path in `processLogicalLine`)

The single-line CALL path (terminated by a period or `END-CALL` on the same line) does **not** return early from `processLogicalLine` by design — it falls through to `extractProcedure`. If `sortAccum` happens to be active at the same time (which requires invalid COBOL — overlapping SORT and CALL blocks), the CALL line text gets appended to `sortAccum`, potentially producing phantom file-name tokens in SORT edges.

This only manifests on structurally invalid COBOL and is therefore **informational only**.

---

#### Finding 4 — `CopyResolution.library` is captured but never consumed 🟢 LOW (dead code)

**Location:** `cobol-copy-expander.ts` — `CopyResolution` interface and `resolveCopy` function

The `library` field of `CopyResolution` is populated by the resolution logic but is never read by the caller. This means `COPY member IN library` or `COPY member OF library` library qualifiers are parsed and discarded — any disambiguation between identically-named copybooks in different libraries is silently lost.

For a future graph that models library-qualified COPY dependencies (e.g. `COPY CUSTIO IN BATCHLIB`) this is a pre-existing architectural gap. **No immediate action required**, but `library` should either be wired into the node/edge attribution or the field should be removed to avoid giving false assurance that library qualification is handled.

### 🏗️ Architectural Fit Assessment

**Strengths (compiler front-end perspective):**

- The two-phase architecture (preprocessor extracts, processor maps to graph) correctly separates syntactic concerns from semantic graph construction — analogous to a front-end IR lowering pass.
- The `COBOL_STATEMENT_VERBS` single source of truth (shared by `callAccum` flush trigger, `inspectAccum` flush trigger, and `RE_USING_PARAMS` lookahead) is the right pattern for a regex-based tokeniser — changes propagate consistently.
- `programBoundaryStack` + `owningModuleId()` correctly models COBOL nested-program scoping as a stack — the right data structure for a block-scoped symbol table.
- Two-pass CALL/CANCEL resolution (`<unresolved>:PROGNAME` synthetic IDs) correctly defers link resolution until all nodes exist, matching the linker-resolution step in compiled languages.
- Area A / Area B column guards for paragraph detection (`leadingSpaces <= 7`) correctly encode COBOL fixed-format layout rules — without this, every `DISPLAY` statement could be misidentified as a paragraph name.

**Residual concerns:**

- The regex pipeline is a hand-rolled lexer with no formal grammar. This is appropriate for the stated scope (graph extraction from legacy COBOL, not full compilation), but the lack of a token stream means certain statement boundaries are context-dependent on accumulator state rather than syntax. The `COBOL_STATEMENT_VERBS` set is the de-facto token classifier; keeping it exhaustive is important for correctness.
- Free-format (`>>SOURCE FREE`) detection is a single-pass flag — no column-range validation is applied in free-format mode. This is acceptable given that free-format COBOL is rare in the legacy corpus this tool targets.
- The `RE_INITIALIZE` single-target gap (Finding 1) is the only remaining medium-severity data-flow accuracy issue. All other new findings are low-severity edge cases.

### 1. The benchmarks job: a third baseline guard

`test(bench): re-baseline the emit-persistence byte-identity fingerprint`

`bench/emit-persistence/baselines.json` is the same class of guard as `scope-capture` and `receiver-resolution`, and it was still red after those two were rebaselined:

```
[emit-persistence --check] FAIL: byte-identity fingerprint drift
  (got 4ee15e74…, expected 69e9182a…)
```

Cause is this branch's own `isDetail` column on `PROPERTY_SCHEMA` — `streamAllCSVsToDisk` writes one more header field. Verified header-only rather than regenerated on faith: dumping every CSV the bench emits on both trees and diffing per file (name, byte length, sha256) gives an identical file set at 35 CSVs, 34 byte-identical, and `property.csv` growing 68 → 77 bytes. The synthetic graph mints no Property nodes, so **not one data row moved** — which is what that fingerprint exists to catch. Both timing gates were green throughout.

**Worth knowing: step 11 aborts the job, so steps 12 and 13 have executed zero times across eleven benchmark-job attempts on this branch.** They aren't guards that pass, they're guards with no result. I ran both locally against the fixed branch — `measure-streaming.mjs --check` PASS, and the cross-language pipeline benchmarks 8 files / 13 tests passed — but this push is the first time CI will actually run them.

### 2. Call flow got slower, and the cause is older than this PR

`perf(processes): build each trace key once, not once per comparison`

`deduplicateTraces` has held its `join('->')` **inside** the `some()` callback since long before this branch, so every kept trace's key is rebuilt against every candidate — `O(T*U)` joins of `O(depth × id-length)` characters. The allocation, not the substring scan, is the cost.

BFS was hiding it by keeping traces short. D1's switch to depth-first is correct and I'd keep it — `pop()` beats an `O(frontier)` `shift()`, and the frontier becomes bounded by depth instead of breadth — but it takes the walk from 4.3 average steps to 9.4, which roughly doubles both `|unique|` and every key length. Same quadratic, ~6× the work. **The diff didn't add a cost; it removed what was bounding one already there.**

Hoisting the join into a `uniqueKeys` array, measured back to back on one host, 5 reps, 25k callables, production sink path — main → this branch before → after:

| shape | main | before | after |
|---|---|---|---|
| deep_chain | 876.8 ms | 1233.1 ms | **101.9 ms** |
| mixed_cycles | 731.4 ms | 1130.6 ms | **132.8 ms** |
| shallow_wide | 572.5 ms | 531.8 ms | **49.6 ms** |

On the real `gitnexus/src` corpus (11,490 symbols) process detection goes 204 ms → 89 ms *against main*, having been slower than main before. So this doesn't just erase the regression.

Output is unchanged, which is the property that matters: swapping the file back and forth and diffing every non-timing field across all sixteen shape × scale × sink-variant configurations gives no difference, and the real corpus returns the same 936 processes / 4,648 steps either way.

### 3. One typing hole

`fix(processes): type the parse-output read as ParseOutput`

The R3-6 sink read declared its own structural shape instead of naming `ParseOutput`, making it the only one of five parse consumers not bound to the real type. Since `getPhaseOutput` is a raw `as T` cast, a local shape checks nothing at runtime and only severs the compile-time link — renaming `allFetchCalls` would still compile here and silently detect zero sinks forever. Confirmed with a `tsc --noEmit --strict` run over exactly that rename. Also brings the `@deps` docblock back in line with the deps array.

### Two things I did not change

**A pre-existing separator bug in the same function.** `'X->AA->B'.includes('A->B')` is `true`, so in principle a trace can be deleted as a sub-path of a chain it never appears in. One-line fix (pad both keys with `->`).

I expected this to change process counts and it does not. Measured, not assumed: with the padding applied, `gitnexus/src` returns the same 936 processes / 4,648 steps, and all sixteen synthetic shape × scale × sink configurations are identical too. Zero delta everywhere I could measure. The reason is that the collision needs one node id to be a proper suffix of another at a `->` boundary, and ids end in `:name:line`, so it essentially cannot happen on real input. It's a latent robustness fix, not a live defect — filing it separately at low priority rather than widening this PR.

**R3-6 buys nothing measurable on this repo.** The corpus reports `fetchCallSites: 0, ormQuerySites: 0`, and the live index has 0 `FETCHES` and 0 `QUERIES` edges; `pr(real sinks)` and `pr(no sinks)` are byte-identical. The measured deepening (avg step count 4.10 → 4.97, histogram now reaching 10) is entirely D1's BFS→DFS. That's a note on where the feature can pay off, not an objection — but the PR body's framing implies sinks are doing work here, and on this repo they aren't.

**Root cause: the capture required a literal URL.**

```
arguments: (arguments
  [(string (string_fragment) @route.url)
   (template_string) @route.template_url])
```

so `fetch(url)` with a variable matched nothing. Counted against your 47: **44 of them pass a variable**, so 94% produced no site. Your zero is that, not a repo quirk — on `crypto-trading-bot` the same query yields 38 `FETCHES` edges because that repo's outward calls go through `axios.get('/literal')`, which the *other* rule catches.

The URL alternation is now optional. The sink set needs only *where* the program reaches outward, not where to. Route linking is untouched by construction rather than by hope — `processNextjsFetchRoutes` normalizes the URL first and skips anything that yields nothing, so a URL-less entry cannot mint a `FETCHES` edge. **Zero `FETCHES` edges does not imply zero fetch sites.** You state the inference for ORM — "ormPhase returns early on an empty `allORMQueries` and otherwise emits one QUERIES edge per de-duplicated entry, so zero edges implies zero sites" — and for ORM that holds. **2. The guard should count SITES, not edges.** If it keys on `FETCHES`/`QUERIES` edge count it will be confounded by route matching — it can read zero on a corpus with plenty of outward calls and no matching routes, and it can read non-zero while extraction is broken for every variable-URL call, which is exactly the state this issue found. Counting `allFetchCalls` / `allORMQueries` length measures the thing you actually care about, and is what makes it fail loudly for the right reason.

Neither changes the fix or your diagnosis — the extractor was blind to 44 of 47 calls and that is now closed. It only changes what a future guard should assert.

Confirmed on a native macOS runner (Darwin, Node v26.5.0) against the current helper.

```text
exit=1
evidence-provenance: Safe generated-plan writes require Linux /proc/self/fd and O_DIRECTORY/O_NOFOLLOW; refusing an unanchored write
artifact: absent
```

This is specifically the descriptor-path backend, not missing open flags: Node exposes both `O_DIRECTORY=1048576` and `O_NOFOLLOW=256` here, but `/proc/self/fd` is absent. The writer then depends on `/proc/self/fd/<fd>` / `/proc/<pid>/fd/<fd>` for traversal and publication, plus Linux `renameat2(RENAME_NOREPLACE)`, so relaxing only `requireDescriptorAnchoring()` would not be safe or sufficient.

One test-coverage gap is relevant: `evidence-provenance-helper.test.ts` sets `SAFE_WRITE_FIXTURES = process.platform === 'linux' ? describe : describe.skip`, so the complete writer suite is skipped on macOS. A patch should add a Darwin backend and run the same create/replace/race/preservation cases there, while keeping no-replace publication and symlink-parent rejection as invariants. I can test a proposed backend on native macOS.

Thanks for the very detailed report — the atomic `git add -A && git commit` losing 6 of 16 files is a great data point, and it's what made this worth chasing properly. I tried to reproduce it and I don't think `analyze` is the process mutating your index. Details below so you can check my reasoning.

## `analyze` never runs an index-writing git command in 1.6.9

I pulled the exact artifact you're running (`npm pack gitnexus@1.6.9`, published 2026-07-04) and inventoried every `git` invocation in the shipped `dist/`, `hooks/`, and `scripts/`:

```
rev-parse (HEAD, --abbrev-ref, --show-toplevel, --git-common-dir, --is-inside-work-tree)
config --get remote.origin.url / core.excludesFile
symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD
rev-list --count
merge-base --is-ancestor
diff
```

No `git status`, and no `add` / `commit` / `reset` / `update-index` / `read-tree` anywhere in the package. The only command in that list that takes `index.lock` and rewrites the index is `git diff` — and in 1.6.9 that lives in exactly two places: the `detect_changes` MCP tool and the wiki generator's commit-range diff. Neither runs as part of `analyze`.

## Reproduction attempt

Test repo plus a linked worktree, both registered in a scratch `GITNEXUS_HOME`, with a `git` shim first on `PATH` logging `pid | cwd | argv` for every invocation. Full `analyze` on the main repo in the background while the worktree ran `git add -A batchN/` (16 files per round) in a tight loop for the whole duration:

```
rounds=2287  lost_rounds=0
git calls with cwd inside the worktree: 0
```

Every git command `analyze` issued had `cwd` = the repo being analyzed. That matters here: a linked worktree has its own index at `.git/worktrees/<name>/index`, so even an index-refreshing command in the main checkout cannot disturb it.

I also checked the second half of the report: after a full `analyze`, 0 of 300 source files had a changed mtime. `analyze` writes `.gitnexus/`, `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, and `.claude/` — nothing under `src/`. One thing it does touch in the shared git dir is `$GIT_DIR/info/exclude`, where it appends `.gitnexus/` — but only from the main checkout (a worktree's `.git` is a file, so the directory stat short-circuits) and only once, since the append is idempotent.

## What I think you actually hit

`pkill -f gitnexus` kills the MCP server too, not just the backgrounded `analyze`. `detect_changes` runs `git diff` in the target repo — and its `worktree` parameter means that diff can be pointed straight at one of your linked worktrees. `git diff` refreshes the index and writes it back under `index.lock`; if it reads the index before your `git add` commits its version and writes after, your staged entries are lost. That is the classic index lost-update, and it matches your symptom exactly, including `git check-ignore` reporting the files as not ignored.

If you can, two things would settle it:

1. Was an MCP server / agent session live at the time, and did anything call `detect_changes` (or `gitnexus status`) against those worktrees?
2. `GIT_TRACE=1` on a failing `git add`, plus `ls -l .git/worktrees/<name>/index` before and after.

## Fix going in regardless

Your "should be strictly read-only toward the target repo's git state" expectation is the right bar, and we don't currently meet it: there is no `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0` / `--no-optional-locks` anywhere in the codebase. Every read-only git spawn should set it so none of them can ever take `index.lock` — that covers `detect_changes`' diff, the wiki diff, and the `git status --porcelain` dirty check that `main` has since added. Tracking that as its own change.

## Why the quoted root cause reads as live but isn't

The `interpret.ts` snippet in the report is accurate — `case 'from'` really does still return `kind: 'named'` unconditionally. That is deliberate: the classification is *reclassified after target resolution*, not at parse time. `interpretPythonImport` only reads syntax; it has no file list, so it cannot know whether `Y` names a submodule.

The decision happens in the `isNamespaceImport` hook on the `ScopeResolver` contract, which Python wires to `isPythonImportedModule` (`src/core/ingestion/languages/python/import-target.ts`). That function reconstructs `targetRaw + '.' + importedName`, resolves the leading-dot relative form against the importing file's directory, and flips the edge to `namespace` when the resolved target is `<path>.py` or `<path>/__init__.py` — which is exactly the check the report proposes, just one layer downstream of where it was looked for.

## Review corrections — two findings retracted, one understated

Follow-up to [the tri-review above](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/pull/2929#pullrequestreview-4914130187). Acting on its findings put every claim back under a runtime, and three of them did not hold up. Correcting them here because leaving a wrong number in a maintainer-signed inline comment is worse than the original miss — and because two of them are the same defect class the review itself was about: a measurement judged against the wrong baseline.

### 1. RETRACTED — "`endsWith(search, endPosition)` is 20x slower than the one-argument form"

Posted inline on `package-dir-index.ts`, `csharp.ts` and `go.ts`. **It does not reproduce.** The 37.68 ns vs 1.87 ns comparison behind it had an unfair baseline: the one-argument call it measured against failed the length/last-char precheck and early-exited without ever comparing. On identical work with identical hit counts (2001 directories, 668 matches, Node 22.18.0, best-of-80 after 300 warmup passes):

| form | ns/candidate |
|---|---|
| `D.endsWith(P)` — 1-arg | 8.15 |
| `D.endsWith(P, D.length)` — 2-arg | 8.55 |
| `D.startsWith(P, pos)` | 8.54 |
| `D.slice(…).endsWith(…)` | 10.65 |

A wash, ~1.05x — not 20x. Two of the agents doing the fix refused to write the number into a production comment because they could not reproduce it, which is the right instinct and is why it never shipped. The source comments now carry only reproduced figures.

### 2. RETRACTED — "two machines can produce different import edges for byte-identical repositories"

Posted in the review body and on the `java/import-target.ts` inline comment. The premise is true and the conclusion is false. `glob('**/*')` really is `readdir`-derived and unsorted — but that is not what reaches the resolver. `filesystem-walker.ts:89` canonicalizes at the scan boundary:

```ts
// Filesystem/glob traversal order is not stable across filesystems or repeated
// scans. Canonicalize once at the scan boundary so every downstream phase sees
// the same repository order.
entries.sort((left, right) => (left.path < right.path ? -1 : left.path > right.path ? 1 : 0));
```

and `test/unit/filesystem-walker-order.test.ts` pins it. I confirmed glob's unsorted output without checking what consumed it.

**What survives:** the tie-break is still file-set iteration order, it is still unpinned by any test, and this PR still moved 149 of those choices. That half of the finding stands and is now gated — the reproducibility framing around it does not.

### 3. UNDERSTATED — the concat removal is worth more than reported

Reported as 2.0–2.7x. Measured on the shipped predicate: `matchingDirs` 32.58 → 8.22 ns/candidate, **3.96x**. The `~92–128 B/candidate` allocation figures should be treated as unverified — heap-delta was GC noise and V8's sampling profiler attributed 0 B to both forms, so the shipped comments cite timings only.

### 4. Corrected in passing

- The census class is real but its count over the bench corpus is **zero** — the corpus contains no instance, so the fingerprint never gated it. Reported as "147 in a 4000-corpus fuzz"; this bench's own generator hits it 4–12 times per 4000 repositories. The zero is the finding, not a reprieve, and the class is now pinned by a unit test instead.
- The compaction gate needed to be a **ceiling**, not the floor the review suggested. Compaction reclaims, so losing it makes the retained reading *grow* (+12.57%) — a floor cannot see that in any sizing.
- V8's growth steps are 1 → 19 → 46 → 86. The review said the old `1 → 17 → 41` model mis-sized the saving by ~2x; at 40 files it is **6x**.

### Unchanged

Both P1s stand as posted and are addressed in `d1e70eca5`: the "filtered downstream" claim is false for File→File `IMPORTS` edges, and tier 3 preempting tier 4 turns a bound answer into an unbound candidate list. So does the dead-`importResolver` finding — re-verified independently, including that the sole production caller of `finalizeScopeModel` does not pass the workspace its adapter's docblock claims it is threaded through.

### 🔴 Function-local imports are never recognized as deferred in the production pipeline — **valid, fixed**

Confirmed exactly as described. `finalize-algorithm.ts:295` publishes every file's finalized edges as `linkedByScope.set(file.moduleScope, …)`, so the map `emitImportEdges` receives holds one bucket per *file*, keyed by that file's `Module` scope. The walk looking for an enclosing `Function` started at a `Module` and returned `false` every time, for every import in the tree. Python's `def f(): from x import Y` was still emitted as an initialization dependency, and this repository's one Python cycle — whose own comment reads *"Kept lazy to avoid a module cycle"* — was still reported.

The unit tests passed because they hand-built `new Map([['fn', …]])`, a shape the pipeline cannot produce. That is the same defect this PR exists to fix, one level up: a gate whose fixture asserts a shape the system never emits. The commit message for `f3c147f2` claimed the Python case was covered; it wasn't.

Fixed by deciding position where it is still known rather than trying to recover it downstream. Scope-extractor Pass 3 resolves each `@import.` anchor to its innermost scope and walks ancestors — `positionIndex` and `scopeTree` were already in scope there and already threaded into Passes 4 and 5. It travels as `ParsedImport.runsOnlyWhenCalled` → `finalize-algorithm` → `ImportEdge`, the same route `typeOnly` takes. `isInsideFunction`, `MAX_SCOPE_DEPTH` and the `scopeDefers` hoist are deleted rather than left as a dead helper.

New `test/unit/scope-resolution/function-local-import-chain.test.ts` drives real Python and Rust source through provider → extractor → finalize → emitter. **Reinstating the shipped emitter fails it 5/10** — verified independently — which is the property the old tests could not have had.

Two consequences worth recording: the PR body's "11 → 1" was aspirational when written (the code delivered 11 → 2, since the Python cycle survived); it is accurate now. And `SCHEMA_BUMP` had to move 60 → 62, because `ParsedImport` gained optional fields that `parsedfile-store.ts` serializes generically — a warm cache would have replayed untagged imports and made the whole branch a silent no-op on incremental analyze. #2864's ledger entry describes that trap in as many words.

Mixed-pair precedence is now one test per independent signal — `dynamic-resolved` vs initializing, function-local vs initializing — plus one carrying all three.

Confirmed. `expandWildcard` builds fresh `wildcard-expanded` edges rather than spreading (three fields differ per exported name) and copied neither flag, so a function-local `use crate::m::*` was tagged correctly on the base edge and lost the tag before the graph bridge. Both flags now travel through the expansion.

`typeOnly` is unreachable there today — `export type *` is unparseable by the vendored grammar, which the `wildcard` variant documents — and is carried anyway with a comment saying so, since the next reader would otherwise delete it as dead.

The gating case needed care, and this is worth recording: the chain harness stubbed `expandsWildcardTo: () => []`, which makes expansion a no-op returning the original edge. A wildcard test written against that stub passes whether or not the fix is present. The harness now returns the finalized edges alongside the reason, and the case asserts two `wildcard-expanded` edges both carrying the flag — so expansion is proven to have run. Removing the fix fails it; verified independently.

### 🔴 Update the cache-version pin when bumping SCHEMA_BUMP — **valid, fixed**

Correct, and it would have been a guaranteed CI failure. `incremental-parse-cache.test.ts` pinned 60 while the constant moved to 62. I found it by running only the targeted suites after the bump, having run the full suite before it.

Both now move together, and the pin names both neighbours rather than just the predecessor: 60 is what `origin/main` holds, so a rebase that drops this branch's bump lands there, and 61 is PR #2935's live claim, so a renumber reaching for "main + 1" collides with it.

### 🔴 C/C++ preprocessor includes are mislabeled as deferred imports — **valid, fixed**

Correct, and it is the failure direction that matters: `#include` is a compile-time textual splice, so a cycle formed by one is real and was being *suppressed*, not invented.

Fixed with a provider capability, `LanguageProvider.importsSplicedAtCompileTime`, rather than a language check in shared code — AGENTS.md forbids naming languages in `src/core/ingestion/` pipeline code. It only ever withholds deferral, so an undeclared provider is unchanged. `(preproc_include) @import.statement` appears in exactly two scope queries (`languages/c/query.ts`, `languages/cpp/query.ts`) and the flag is set on exactly the two providers that own them; the other 14 providers declaring `interpretImport` are untouched. C++'s only other Pass-3 import form, `using ns::name`, is compile-time name lookup and is correct under the same flag.

Gated by a test asserting the C include is plain **and**, in the same run, that a Python function-local import is still deferred — so "nothing is ever tagged" cannot pass it.

### 🔴 Preserve typeOnly for default imports — **refuted, but it found a real gap**

`ParsedImport` has no `default` kind. The decomposer's `default` case returns `kind: 'alias'` (with `...typeOnly`), and `typeOnlyFor` already covered `alias`. All seven `...typeOnly` spread sites in `interpret.ts` map onto the four kinds the helper handled, so nothing was being dropped. `import type Foo from './m'` was already asserted as `(type-only)` at `type-only-import-chain.test.ts:104-105`, predating this review.

But nothing pinned the *correspondence*, which is exactly why the question was open — so it is now pinned twice. A runtime table asserts which kind each erasable spelling arrives as, plus that its runtime twin arrives as the **same** kind without the flag (which is why erasure cannot be inferred from `kind`). And the helper's `default:` arm is gone: the four erasable kinds are listed and the rest go through a compile-time exhaustiveness assertion. Adding `typeOnly` to a variant the helper ignores is now `TS2345`, and adding a new kind is `TS2322 … not assignable to 'never'` — both verified by mutation.

Good finding even though the specific claim was wrong.

### 🟡 Changed symbol `extract` with 2 external callers — **checked, no action**

Signature unchanged; the new capability is an optional field on the hooks object, read once in Pass 3, defaulting to current behaviour.

## 🔴 #9 — `presence` is declared readonly but is mutated

Not the case. Only two of the three properties are readonly:

```ts
const pairs = new Map<
  string,
  { readonly sourceFile: string; readonly targetFile: string; presence: ImportPresence }
>();
```

`presence` is intentionally mutable — the dedup pass lowers it as stronger evidence arrives, which is the mechanism that makes an initializing edge win a mixed pair. The asymmetry is deliberate: the two path fields are fixed once the key exists, the rank is not.

If it were readonly this would be `TS2540`, and `npx tsc --noEmit` is clean in both packages.

## 🔴 #8 — C++ `using` declarations

Refuted, and the direction matters: the proposed change moves toward **hiding** cycles.

`importsExecuteWhereWritten: false` means *position does not defer this import* — the edge is treated as an initialization dependency. The finding argues a function-local `using` should keep the deferred classification because it "only changes compile-time name lookup and does not load or initialize".

That premise is right and the conclusion inverts. "Deferred" in this model means *runs later, at call time*. A `using` inside a function body does not run later — it is resolved at compile time exactly where it sits, the same as one at namespace scope. There is nothing to defer. Classifying it deferred would assert that the dependency materializes only when the function is called, which is false for every C++ construct.

The failure directions are not symmetric, which is what settles it. Treating a compile-time form as initializing **over-reports** — a cycle is shown that a reader can dismiss. Treating it as deferred **suppresses** — a real cycle is dropped and nobody sees it. The capability's own docblock records that asymmetry, and this is exactly the case it was written for: `dca5f4b0a` flagged `using ns::name` as C++'s other Pass-3 import form and classified it under the same flag deliberately, not by oversight.

The narrower, genuinely open question is whether a `using` should produce an `IMPORTS` edge at all, since it names a symbol rather than pulling in a translation unit. That is about edge *emission*, not about this flag, and it would change the graph for every C++ repository — its own change.

## 🔴 #10 — Non-JSON handling of the `none` response

The mechanism is real; the crash is not, because the guard is already there:

```ts
// A rendering guard, not an exit-code decision — `output()` owns that. An
// error payload carries no `cycles` array, so the prose branch below would
// throw on it; print the structured payload and stop.
if (result?.error) {
  output(result);
  return;
}
```

`{ error, truncated }` has `error`, so it never reaches `result.cycles.map(...)`.

What the finding did surface is a real coverage gap: the existing error cases cover **JSON** mode and a **thrown** error, and neither exercises the branch that renders prose. `9baf9f649` adds that case, and I verified it gates — deleting the guard fails exactly this test and nothing else:

```

               → "prints the safety-limit error in PROSE mode instead of throwing on the missing cycle list"
```

Good catch even though the code was already correct.

## P1

- **generator.ts:1816 hash timing** — ✅ Fixed. The `document_plan.json` content hash is now compared with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` over equal-length buffers.
- **publisher.ts:244 lock race** — ⚠️ Not reproduced (believed invalid). The lock is taken with `fs.open(lockPath, 'wx')` (O_EXCL). `lock.close()` only closes the fd — it does **not** delete the file or its directory entry — so between `close()` and `unlink()` the lock file still exists and any other publisher's `wx` open returns `EEXIST`. The `unlink` therefore always removes the current publisher's own lock, never a "replacement". Happy to add a defensive PID check on unlink if you'd still like it, but the described race shouldn't occur. (A separate, real concern is a stale lock after a crash — different from what was reported; can follow up.)
- **engineering-wiki overall-architecture** — ✅ Fixed. `validateEngineeringDiagram` now accepts an `unknown` block as the prompt-permitted degrade when relationship evidence is insufficient (the "emit unknown instead of inventing a diagram" path now succeeds), while still rejecting responses with neither a diagram nor an unknown block.

- **validator required evidence across sections** — ✅ Fixed. `missingRequirements` now checks evidence actually cited by *that* section (via `evidenceIdsForSection`) rather than the whole bundle; sections carrying an `unknown` (needs-human) degrade are exempt, since the degrade already signals insufficient evidence.

Added `validateDiagramPolicy` (allowed / maxNodes / kinds) invoked for all non-default profiles; `WriteSectionRequest` now carries `diagramPolicy` and the generator passes it through. - **iso-42010 external-calls** — ✅ Fixed. Pulled every comment on this PR — 6 issue comments, 6 reviews, 13 inline — and triaged them against what this tool actually is: **a static analyser building a code graph, not a compiler, transpiler or V8.** That framing changes several verdicts, so it is stated explicitly below.

## The bar for "reliable module resolution" here

A compiler resolves in order to *emit*, against an installed, buildable project, and may refuse to proceed. GitNexus resolves in order to *describe*, and:

1. must work on a checkout that was **never installed and never built** — `node_modules/` and `dist/` are not indexed;
2. must never fabricate an edge, because a wrong edge is indistinguishable from a real one downstream (this is #2953 itself);
3. may resolve **less** than tsc without being wrong — a missing edge is a gap, an invented one is a defect;
4. needs nothing tsc does for typing: conditional `exports` per runtime, `lib`/`target`, declaration emit.

So findings get judged on "does the project declare this, and can we read it without a build" — not on "would tsc do it".

## Round 2 — four new findings, all valid, all fixed

| finding | verdict | why it matters *here* |
|---|---|---|
| `exports`/`imports` **arrays** skipped | valid | `["./dist/x.js", "./src/x.ts"]` is how a workspace package says "built output, or source". `dist/` is not indexed and the build may never have run, so **the source arm is the only one we can use** — and skipping arrays dropped the declaration entirely, making the package look as though it exported no subpaths |
| exact `paths` pattern didn't outrank a wildcard | valid | `a` and `a*` both match `a` at prefix length 1, so tsc's exact-wins rule was left to declaration order |
| package-form `extends` refused | valid | not *indexing* `node_modules` ≠ not *reading* it; a shared internal base is where a monorepo puts its `paths` |
| CodeQL: `replace('*', …)` ×2 | valid | ⬅️ this was the failing CodeQL check |

**On the CodeQL one** — the behaviour was already correct: Node subpath patterns and tsconfig `paths` both allow **at most one** `*`, so replacing the first occurrence *is* the spec. But `String.replace` with a string needle says that only by accident and reads as the replace-all footgun. `substituteStar` now slices at the known index and states the rule.

**On package-form `extends`** — worth reporting because the test contradicted my first assumption. It is now read from disk, walking `node_modules` upward the way Node does, and absent on an un-installed checkout it degrades to whatever the extending config declared itself. But the test pins what tsc *actually* does with such a base rather than what I expected:

> `extends` never rebases `baseUrl`. A package base declaring `"baseUrl": "src"` means `node_modules/@acme/tsconfig/src`, not the consuming repo's `src`.

So a published base rarely contributes aliases a repo's own files resolve through — and the `@tsconfig/*` family, which sets `target` and `lib` and never `paths`, is a no-op here either way. Reading it is still correct; the expectation that it would unlock aliases was not.

## Deliberately not doing

- **conditional `exports` resolution per runtime** (`node` vs `browser` vs `import`/`require`). We collect the string leaves of every condition and try them in order. A compiler must pick one branch; an analyser wants the union, because the graph should show the file regardless of which runtime the consumer picked.

- **type-only resolution** (`typesVersions`, `@types/*`). Irrelevant to a file-level import graph.

Each of these makes us resolve *less* than tsc, never differently.

**1. `exports` map that omits the root still answered a bare import.** When a manifest declares `exports`, that map is the package's *entire* public interface — Node ignores `main` outright and refuses any subpath the map doesn't list. I already honoured that restriction for **subpaths** and not for the **package root**, which is the same rule. So `{"exports": {"./feature": "./src/feature.ts"}}` still resolved a bare `@repo/pkg` to `main` or `src/index`, an edge for an import that doesn't resolve in the real project. Legacy and conventional root candidates are now offered only when there is no `exports` field at all.

That one was an inconsistency inside my own code, not a missing feature — the bot caught an asymmetry I'd written two screens apart.

**2. An empty tsconfig was dropped, so an ancestor's `baseUrl` governed its files.** A config declaring neither `baseUrl` nor `paths` was skipped rather than kept as an empty scope, so `tsconfigFor` fell through to an enclosing config. A package whose own tsconfig declares no `baseUrl` — meaning its non-relative specifiers are *package lookups* — silently inherited the repo root's aliases. An empty scope is the accurate answer for such a file, and only a scope can express it.

Both are pinned at the level they broke: the manifest arms assert what `readManifest` **produces**, not a hand-built package, because "the resolver honours empty entries" and "the loader produces empty entries" are different claims and only the second was at fault.

## One deviation from the acceptance criteria here, stated up front

This ticket proposes mirroring C#'s #1881 shape — *gate* the stripping loop on declared-package evidence. The fix goes further and **resolves from** the declarations instead of fencing a guess:

```
com.example.model.User  →  package com.example.model declares User
java.util.List          →  no file declares package java.util  →  null
```

The reason is that the gate leaves the underlying question unanswered. `resolveJavaImportTarget` was matching path *shape*, and path shape is a convention Java does not enforce — `weird/path/User.java` declaring `package com.example;` **is** `com.example.User`, and `com/example/User.java` declaring nothing is in the default package and importable as nothing at all. A gate in front of the stripping loop still gets both of those wrong; reading the `package` header gets them right and makes the JDK case fall out for free.

It also cost nothing extra. As this ticket notes, the evidence is *"already parsed out of the `.java` files"* — `getJavaPackageFact(filePath)` is populated by the time resolution runs, and nothing read it. So there is no new I/O, no `pom.xml` and no `build.gradle` parsing.

## Consequence for the last acceptance bullet

That bullet asks for `java-import-target-parity.test.ts` to have its expectations **updated**, explicitly so the change is visible rather than silent.
