Submitted PR #4105 implementing configurable max iterations, token usage tracking, approximate USD cost estimation, and per-question token budget controls for Nexus AI (`gitnexus-web`).

**Approach:**
- Replaced the hardcoded `recursionLimit: 50` in `streamAgentResponse` with configurable `maxIterations` (default `8`, clamped `[1, 50]`, mapped to `2 * maxIterations + 1`) and handled LangGraph `GRAPH_RECURSION_LIMIT` exits as structured `{ type: 'budget_exceeded', reason: 'max_iterations' }` events.
- Extracted and deduplicated `usage_metadata` / `response_metadata` per AI message across both `'messages'` chunks and `'values'` snapshots so streamed turns never double-count tokens.
- Enforced `tokenBudget` (`0` = unlimited) via a linked `AbortController` that keeps user Stop cancellation independent, marks interrupted tool cards `stopped`, and appends a localized notice (`en` and `zh-CN`).
- Added `pricing.ts` for cloud model USD cost estimation while showing `Local (free)` for Ollama and omitting fabricated dollar amounts for unknown custom models.

1. **Index that matches neither image.** In `filesIndexedAsPreImage`, a file whose recorded hash matches neither the new side nor the old blob falls through and keeps the post-image ranges, and `queryDegraded` stays false. The ranges are then wrong for the graph but the result still reads as complete, so the gate can report `low` on the wrong symbols. Hi @muzman123 — I hit the same thing and have an implementation working locally, so here is the diagnosis and the one design decision I would like to check before opening the PR. (@victrvondoom has also claimed this one — if you would rather split the work, say so and I will adjust; otherwise I will open the PR.)

**Diagnosis.** The cache is skipped on Windows in `gitnexus/src/core/analyzer-identity.ts`: `currentUid()` returns `null` there, so `isOwnedPrivateDirectory()` always returns `false` and `persistIdentityCache()` returns without writing. The identity itself was never the obstacle — `readCacheFile()` already tolerates `uid === null` and only requires the *directory* to be private, which is exactly the missing Windows equivalent of `stat.uid`/`stat.mode`.

**What I implemented**

- Default location `%USERPROFILE%\.gitnexus\analyzer-identity`, as you proposed. One wrinkle: it has to be derived from the OS profile rather than from `HOME`/`GITNEXUS_HOME`, because an existing test requires the default cache to survive an isolated `HOME`/`GITNEXUS_HOME` — the path must not follow relocated state.
- On every use the privacy of that directory is proven and the directory is locked so only the current user, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` can reach it. If the proof fails, the cache is skipped, exactly as today.
- A directory that turns out not to be private is discarded and used empty afterwards. Only files whose names match the cache file format are removed, and they are removed only after the lock succeeded.
- Mac/Linux are untouched: same default locations, same proof, same behaviour.

**One deviation, and why.** `icacls` cannot answer the question completely. An owner may always rewrite the access-control list of the object it owns, so a directory owned by somebody else is not private no matter what its ACL says — that is precisely why the POSIX side requires `stat.uid === uid` and not only the mode bits. `icacls` cannot report the owner: `icacls <dir> /save` writes only the DACL section of the SDDL (there is no `O:` owner section) and plain `icacls <dir>` prints account names, which are localized.

The probe therefore asks the OS through `powershell.exe` using the .NET ACL API. It resolves every identity to a SID — the language-independent check you asked for — and reports the owner in the same round trip. The directory is passed to the script in an environment variable, never interpolated into the script text, so a path containing quotes or commas cannot change the command.

The cost is that call: one PowerShell start-up per run, 0.50–0.57 s measured on my machine — the same ~0.5 s you measured — against the ~12 ms you measured for `icacls`. On your numbers that is `status` 9.3 s → ~2.2 s and `analyze` 20.2 s → ~6.3 s instead of 1.7 s/5.8 s. The lock and the check that follows it share one process, so a run never pays for more than one start-up. If you would rather have the 12 ms, the DACL half can move to `icacls /save` (SID-based SDDL) and only the owner check would still need the OS — say the word and I will switch.

**Also:** the per-user Windows directory now keeps only the three newest cache entries, so the ~8 MB files cannot pile up over updates, and a temporary file left behind by an interrupted write is removed once it is a day old. A directory you point `GITNEXUS_ANALYZER_IDENTITY_CACHE_DIR` at is never pruned.

Does this match what you had in mind? I will open the PR with the implementation unless someone is already far along.

If another principal able to modify the containing directory replaces the checked directory with a junction between those processes, the lock script follows the supplied path without rechecking it and applies the cache ACL to the junction target. The lock operation therefore needs its own reparse-point check immediately before changing the ACL. I'd like to take what's left of this one.

NDJSON streaming (#732) and the chat-only mode for large repos (#2185) fixed most of this. One failure is left for downloads that take longer than 120 s, such as "Load graph anyway" on a large repo. `fetchGraph` passes its 120 s timeout to `fetchWithTimeout` (`gitnexus-web/src/services/backend-client.ts:860`), and that `AbortSignal.timeout` keeps running while the body streams. So a graph that is still receiving rows gets cut off at 120 s, however steadily the rows arrive.

The error isn't mapped either. `fetchWithTimeout` only turns a `TimeoutError` into a timeout `BackendError` while waiting for the response (line 622). An abort during `reader.read()` in `parseNdjsonGraphResponse` (line 960) reaches `connectToServer` as a raw `DOMException`, and it rethrows it (line 1363).

Repro: a local server streams NDJSON node rows steadily for 150 s. The client does what `fetchGraph` does: `fetch()` with `AbortSignal.timeout(120_000)`, the timeout mapped around the `fetch()` call only, and the body read line by line after it.

    0.1s headers: 200
    120.0s body read threw DOMException TimeoutError: "The operation was aborted due to timeout" after 38540 rows; last row arrived at 120.0s

On GitNexus itself (136K nodes, 438K edges, 228 MB of NDJSON), a local download finishes in 44.5 s with a Node client, about 12.9K rows/s. So hitting the limit locally takes roughly 1.5M rows, or a slower client or link: the browser parses rows on its main thread, and `serve --host` allows remote backends.

Plan:

- Swap the whole-request timeout on the graph download for an idle timeout that resets on every chunk. A server that goes quiet for 120 s still fails, but a stream that keeps sending rows finishes.
- Turn a timeout during the body read into the same timeout `BackendError` that `fetchWithTimeout` already throws, so the UI shows the usual message. Caller cancellation stays as it is today.
- Tests in gitnexus-web with a mocked streamed response: rows that keep arriving past the old limit finish, a stalled stream fails with a timeout `BackendError`, and the caller's abort still cancels.

The change stays in `backend-client.ts` and its tests.

@azizur100389 thanks for the review and the exact-head probe. The getter case is fixed in 7ea090d1.

**P2 (getter → stale route).** The root cause is wider than getters. `flattenObjectLiteral` only models `key: value` pairs, so anything else in the literal can change what a member read returns. A table is now folded only when its literal is plain: pairs with static (`property_identifier` or string), distinct keys, and plain nested tables. A getter, setter, method, spread, computed key, shorthand, repeated key or `__proto__` entry makes the whole table untrusted. This check runs before the existing escape scan (alias, call argument, export, subscript, write).

**Open question (regression test with runtime/extraction parity).** I added a parity table test. Each case evaluates the table literal at runtime with `new Function`, reads the same member the route uses, and then requires the extractor to emit exactly `GET <runtime value>` for plain tables, or nothing at all for every other shape:

| Table | Runtime | Extracted |
|---|---|---|
| `{ A: "/plain" }`, nested, quoted key, `as const` | the literal | the same path |
| `{ A: "/stale", get A() { return "/actual"; } }` (top-level and nested) | `/actual` | nothing |
| getter only, computed key, repeated key, `__proto__`, spread | varies | nothing |

### P1 · A valid call to an overloaded function disappears

```ts
export function pick(x: { key: number }): number;
export function pick(x: { key: string }): string;
export function pick(x: { key: string | number }) { return x.key; }

export function run(x: { key: string }) { return pick(x); }
```

TypeScript 7.0.2 selects the second overload. The base publishes `run → pick`. The PR publishes zero `CALLS` edges for `run`, so a caller or impact query misses the relationship. The new overload resolver can return `unknown` when several candidates survive its narrowing. That result suppresses the ordinary call fallback.

**Requested change.** Preserve the call edge when every plausible signature belongs to the same implementation. Track uncertainty about the chosen signature separately. Add this fixture alongside a control for an inapplicable call. [Overload resolver](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/blob/209875beef2dedeee25ccc7deb822c0f34ea753f/gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/typescript/function-overloads.ts#L45) · [Existing discussion](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/pull/4084#discussion_r4711018690) · [TypeScript overload definitions](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html#overload-signatures-and-the-implementation-signature)

### P2 · One free-function overload triggers repeated scans of shared globals

An importer that shadows a global name gets a filtered view of the shared bindings. When a free function has overloads, the overload-name index iterates every such view. I measured the production helper using indexes captured from generated TypeScript projects. Each project had one unrelated overloaded free function and one different shadowed name per importer.

| Global names | Importing modules | Entries yielded by filtered views | Additional entries from shared view |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 16 | 16 | 240 | 16 |
| 32 | 32 | 992 | 32 |
| 64 | 64 | 4,032 | 64 |
| 128 | 128 | 16,256 | 128 |

The filtered views yielded `N × (N − 1)` entries when both dimensions equalled `N`. These counts establish quadratic work for this input shape. Its effect on end-to-end indexing time remains unmeasured.

**Requested change.** Collect possible overload names once per underlying global table. Keep each importer’s actual scope lookup and alias handling when resolving a call. Add an operation-count check with distinct shadowed names and an imported alias. [Overload indexing](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/blob/209875beef2dedeee25ccc7deb822c0f34ea753f/gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/typescript/call-arguments.ts#L124) · [Filtered global bindings](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/blob/209875beef2dedeee25ccc7deb822c0f34ea753f/gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/typescript/global-declarations.ts#L49)

### P2 · Two gaps in ECMAScript property-key handling

| Case | Observed on the PR | Requested change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A literal name contains a dot | For an overloaded method named `['a.b']`, TypeScript selects the matching declaration. GitNexus creates the method node but publishes no `CALLS` edge. The qualifier interprets the dot in the name as an owner separator. | Carry the owner and the complete property key separately through lookup. Test a class with both `b` and `['a.b']`. [Capture](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/blob/209875beef2dedeee25ccc7deb822c0f34ea753f/gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/typescript/captures.ts#L463) · [Qualification](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/blob/209875beef2dedeee25ccc7deb822c0f34ea753f/gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/scope-resolution/scope/walkers.ts#L2261) |
| A constant key uses a template or parentheses | `c['run']()` publishes an edge. Both ``c[`run`]()`` and `c[('run')]()` miss it. A method declared with a no-substitution template is also absent from the graph. | Unwrap parentheses and decode template literals with zero substitutions in the declaration and call paths. Keep dynamic template expressions outside this constant-key rule. [Declaration capture](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/blob/209875beef2dedeee25ccc7deb822c0f34ea753f/gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/typescript/query.ts#L574) · [Call capture](https://github.com/abhigyanpatwari/GitNexus/blob/209875beef2dedeee25ccc7deb822c0f34ea753f/gitnexus/src/core/ingestion/languages/typescript/query.ts#L1284) |

The base also missed the dotted and template cases. They are gaps in the coverage of the literal-member support added by this PR. ECMA-262 treats a computed name as one property key. A no-substitution template produces its string value, and parentheses preserve the value of the enclosed expression. [Computed property names, §13.2.5.5](https://tc39.es/ecma262/2026/multipage/ecmascript-language-expressions.html#sec-object-initializer-runtime-semantics-evaluation) · [Template evaluation, §13.2.8.6](https://tc39.es/ecma262/2026/multipage/ecmascript-language-expressions.html#sec-template-literals-runtime-semantics-evaluation) · [Grouping, §13.2.9.2](https://tc39.es/ecma262/2026/multipage/ecmascript-language-expressions.html#sec-grouping-operator-runtime-semantics-evaluation) · [Bracket access, §13.3.3](https://tc39.es/ecma262/2026/multipage/ecmascript-language-expressions.html#sec-evaluate-property-access-with-expression-key)

A class can define both a static `m()` and an instance `['static.m']()`. Node invoked two different methods. TypeScript selected two different declaration positions. Thanks for the careful review and the probes. Both points are addressed at the new head, and the branch is rebased on current main.

**Cypher and storage faults.** Caller Cypher no longer turns every engine failure into a client fault. The read pool now records the LadybugDB exception category that the engine puts at the start of its message (the exception types named in the native binary). Parser, Binder, Catalog, Conversion, Runtime and Overflow errors stay `client`; IO, Buffer manager, Storage, Connection and Copy errors, and any error with no recognized category, are `server`. Your probe, an `IO exception` injected at execute under `cypher`, is now `server`. A sentinel test on a real LadybugDB produces real Parser, Binder, Catalog, Conversion and Runtime errors and fails if the engine stops naming them that way, so a format change cannot silently send everything to `server`. The docs section and the PR description no longer describe this as a blind spot. One common caller mistake carries no category: a `$param` typo or a forgotten `params` makes the engine answer `Parameter x not found.`. The cypher tool now checks, before running the statement, which `$name` references outside string literals, quoted names and comments are missing from `params`; when one is, that uncategorized engine error is classified `client`. Every other uncategorized engine error stays `server`, and the query and its response text are unchanged. A statement with several queries (`Connection Exception: ... multiple statements`) is still `server`, and the docs say so.

**Windows.** The filesystem fault tests now check each error code by injecting it where it is raised, and keep real-filesystem smoke cases that accept the platform's code (`ENOENT` on Windows, the POSIX code elsewhere) while asserting the same fault class. Windows also exposed one real misclassification, a group directory replaced by a file reading as a missing group, which is fixed with its own test.

**Which Windows job covers them.** None did before: the `windows-latest (platform-sensitive)` job runs the explicit list in `gitnexus/scripts/cross-platform-tests.ts`, and these files were not on it. They are now registered there (the native ones under `LBUG_NATIVE`, the filesystem ones under `FILESYSTEM`), so the Windows and macOS shards select them. I could not run them on a Windows machine myself, so that CI job is their first real Windows run.

**1. `op.startsWith('not')` on `op: FilterOp` linked to the enum member.** Enum member nodes had no `isStatic`. TypeScript already sets `separateStaticAndInstanceMethods`, so instance dispatch drops static members, but the TypeScript field extractor never treated `enum_declaration` as a field owner. Enum members are now static readonly fields of the enum object. `FilterOp.eq` and `Color.Red` still resolve. The static-field filter in `pickFirstNonStaticOnly` now applies to reads and writes as well as calls, so `op.eq` on an enum-typed value doesn't link either. A consequence for TypeScript classes: reading or writing a `static` field through an instance (`c.count` on `c: C`, which is TS2576) no longer links.

**2. Vue unique-name fallback.** A new optional `ScopeResolver.excludeEnumMembersFromNameFallback` option. The property-name index tags members owned only by an `Enum`, and the fallback skips them when the reading provider opts in. Vue opts in. An untyped `x.Off` no longer links to `Mode.Off`, and a same-named object key in another file keeps its fallback edge.

Not covered: a call on an enum-typed value inside a `.vue` file. Vue doesn't set `separateStaticAndInstanceMethods`.
